title: On the Expected Maximum Deficit and the Optimal Allocation of Reserves

p.t: Risk measures are central to quantitative risk management (see, e.g., McNeil et al., 2015), but a terminal criterion can miss substantial distress before the evaluation date. Value-at-Risk is generally not coherent (Artzner et al., 1999); when applied to the running maximum it captures the path of losses, but it remains a quantile and does not measure the severity beyond the selected confidence level. The expected maximum deficit instead evaluates the deepest liquidity shortfall attained over the horizon. Ruin theory has long complemented ruin probabilities with measures of deficit severity, including the expected discounted penalty function (Gerber and Shiu, 1998;Gerber et al., 1987) and the maximum severity of ruin (Dickson, 1998;Thampi et al., 2007;Li and Lu, 2013). Related path-dependent indicators and single-period shareholder-deficit measures appear in Trufin et al. (2011), Loisel and Trufin (2014), Sherris (2006) and Kim and Hardy (2009). The finite-horizon expected maximum deficit was considered by Jiang (2015), and Lefèvre et al. (2017) established stochastic comparisons for the classical risk model. Unlike quantities conditional on ruin, the expected maximum deficit combines the probability of exceeding capital with the severity of the excess; it measures the maximum depth, but not the duration, of a liquidity deficit. Against this background, we use the distorted expected maximum deficit to construct monetary capital requirements and reserve-allocation criteria. The process formulation builds on the monetary-risk-measure literature (Cheridito et al., 2005;Föllmer and Penner, 2006;Bielecki et al., 2025), while the fixed-tolerance construction is related to shortfall acceptance sets (Föllmer and Schied, 2002). The main contributions are the proportionaltolerance coherent capital rule and its comparison with direct distorted-supremum capital, the invariance of the marginal-summation allocation under a common increasing distortion, and a dependence-sensitive worst-line allocation criterion. These allocation criteria complement established axiomatic approaches (Tsanakas, 2009;Dhaene et al., 2012) and integrated-surplus allocations (Loisel, 2005).

We also study conditional updating of the capital evaluations and show how the static allocation rules can be reapplied at discrete review dates using conditional future-increment laws and a given total budget. This rolling formulation is an operational implementation of the one-period criteria, rather than a separate intertemporal capital-control problem. In this section, we propose static risk measures evaluated at time zero directly related to the expected maximum deficit over the fixed horizon [0, t]. This maps the mathematical behavior of the deficit into the axiomatic framework of path-dependent risk measures, providing robust tools for static initial risk assessment. Before detailing specific functionals, we first recall the formal definitions of convex and coherent risk measures on the space of unbounded càdlàg processes H 0 , as established by Cheridito et al. (2005). A functional ρ : H 0 → R ∪ {+∞} is called a convex risk measure if it satisfies the following conditions for any X, Y ∈ H 0 : Furthermore, the functional ρ is a coherent risk measure if it is a convex risk measure that additionally satisfies: (v) Positive Homogeneity: ρ(λX) = λρ(X) for any λ ≥ 0. Under positive homogeneity, convexity is mathematically equivalent to subadditivity, i.e., ρ(X + Y ) ≤ ρ(X) + ρ(Y ). We focus on the capital rules generated directly by the expected maximum deficit. Multiplying a monetary risk measure by a scalar generally changes its cash-additivity coefficient; any normalization must therefore be specified as part of the acceptance criterion rather than treated as an innocuous rescaling. The observation applies to each of the three capital measures below; for the implicit measures, however, external anchored scaling is not the same operation as recalibrating A or δ, which changes the underlying acceptance criterion.

To integrate tail risk aversion for a generic continuous-time loss process X ∈ H 0 , one might first consider the raw functional Although the positive part preserves convexity and monotonicity, this functional is not cash additive: injecting deterministic capital reduces the expected deficit nonlinearly. It is therefore a convex penalty, not a monetary risk measure in isolation. To resolve this and restore cash-additivity, we advance the classical shortfall risk framework of Föllmer and Schied (2002). Rather than using the raw functional as the risk measure directly, we use it to define a static acceptance set of risk profiles bounded by a prescribed tolerance. In the following subsections, we demonstrate how bounding this tolerance by either an absolute constant or a proportional capital constraint yields distinct axiomatic properties.

p.s: A convex measure with a fixed risk tolerance
p.t: Rather than using the raw functional as the risk measure directly, we use it to define a static acceptance set of risk profiles bounded by a prescribed deterministic tolerance A > 0: where the expectation E g is evaluated via the Choquet integral with respect to a concave distortion function g. The tolerance A has units of money and represents a budget for the expected depth of the maximum shortfall. It should be calibrated to the firm's risk appetite or stress-testing policy. It is not a measure of deficit duration and does not, by itself, specify statutory reserve constraints. To illustrate the framework and quantify the impact of tail-risk aversion, we evaluate the capital requirements across the proposed risk measures. The examples now span three distinct dimensions that are absent from a single infinitehorizon exponential benchmark: finite-horizon convergence, increased claim-size dispersion through a hyperexponential model, and dependence sensitivity in Example 4.10. Their purpose is to test horizon, marginal-distribution and joint-distribution effects separately. For infinite-horizon exponential claims with µ = 1, all fixed-tolerance values are computed from the piecewise formulas (3.13)-(3.14); reported operational capital is truncated at zero according to (3.11). Many insurance companies operate several distinct lines of business. While decision makers often establish risk limits at the aggregate company level, modern enterprise risk management increasingly defines limits at the granular level of individual business lines to optimize capital efficiency. While capital allocation can be addressed using established marginal principlessuch as the Euler allocation for coherent risk measures or the Aumann-Shapley (AS) allocation for convex risk measures (Tsanakas, 2009)-we explore alternative mathematical formulations targeted specifically at the path-dependent mechanics of the deficit process. In this section, we apply our previously defined risk measures to determine an optimal static allocation of a total reserve u among K distinct lines. Consider K lines of business, where the reserve process for the k-th line is given by R (k) Here, u k is the initial reserve allocated to the k-th line, and L (k) s denotes its aggregate loss up to time s. We denote the running maximum loss for this line as M (k) t = sup 0≤s≤t L (k) s . The corresponding physical ruin probability over the finite horizon [0, t] is defined as ψ k (u k , t) = P M (k) t > u k , and its ultimate ruin probability as To capture the static risk of each individual line, we define the distorted expected maximum deficit tailored for the k-th line by embedding a continuously differentiable, strictly increasing distortion function g k :

At the global company level, the aggregate reserve process is simply the sum of the individual lines, R s = K k=1 R (k) s . Evaluating this at the aggregate level yields the static company-wide risk measure: Because J pool depends on the individual allocations (u 1 , . . . , u K ) only through the total sum of reserves u = K k=1 u k , it does not provide a meaningful mechanism for internal capital allocation among the distinct lines. Thus, we must explore alternative mathematical formulations that lead to intuitive allocation rules. This approach parallels the philosophy of Loisel (2004) and Loisel and Trufin (2014), who studied optimal capital allocations based on the integrated negative part of the surplus, s <0} ds. The appropriate objective depends on whether reserves can be pooled. Method 1 is constructed from marginal line-specific deficits and is suitable for an internal allocation score. Method 2 evaluates the magnitude of the worst line deficit and is appropriate when reserves are legally ring-fenced, transfers are delayed or costly, or management imposes line-level solvency constraints. It is not the deficit of the pooled company. Although Method 2 uses the union of line-level deficit events at each severity threshold, it measures the magnitude of the worst deficit rather than only the occurrence of that union event.

In the following analysis, we define and compare two distinct capital allocation methodologies that arise naturally from the expected maximum deficit: • Method 1 (Marginal Summation): Allocating capital to minimize the sum of the line-specific distorted expected maximum deficits (J marg ). • Method 2 (Worst-Line Maximum Deficit): Allocating capital to minimize the distorted maximum deficit of the minimum-reserve, or worst-line, process (J worst ). The symbols J pool , J marg and J worst are objective functions of an allocation vector, not monetary risk measures acting on a process. This notation separates them from ρ and ρ (t) δ,g .

The dynamic results are local to the selected horizon: the direct conditional evaluation satisfies a supermartingale inequality rather than a recursive tower property, the implicit roots provide frozen-capital adequacy, and the review-date allocation reapplies the static criteria with a given budget. Transaction costs, transfer limits, default resolution and endogenous recapitalization require a separate intertemporal model.

This paper develops capital and reserve-allocation criteria based on the distorted expected maximum deficit, a path-dependent measure that combines the probability and the severity of the largest liquidity shortfall over a chosen horizon. Three capital rules are studied: the direct coherent evaluation of the running maximum, a fixed-tolerance convex monetary measure, and a proportional-tolerance coherent measure. The proportional-tolerance construction is the main capital-measure contribution: it turns an implicit EMD constraint into a coherent rule. The three measures also preserve the increasing-convex-order comparisons inherited from the underlying risk processes. At the portfolio level, the two allocation criteria answer different economic questions. Minimizing the sum of line-specific deficits equalizes marginal distorted ruin probabilities and, when all lines use the same strictly increasing distortion, produces an allocation that is invariant to that distortion. The worst-line criterion instead protects the weakest ringfenced business line. It is convex and depends on the joint loss distribution, so it captures dependence that is absent from the marginal-summation criterion. The exponential and Bernoulli examples illustrate, respectively, its analytical tractability and its sensitivity to dependence. The conditional results show how these static criteria can be updated as information arrives, while also marking the limits of the analysis. The direct distorted-supremum evaluation satisfies a supermartingale inequality, whereas the implicit capital measures retain the weaker expected adequacy of capital fixed at the current information date. Under stationary independent increments, a rolling assessment separates into the realized loss and the static assessment of a future increment. The allocation criteria can therefore be reapplied at review dates using updated conditional laws and the available budget. This provides a practical framework for periodic reassessment, but not a globally optimal recapitalization or dividend policy. The infinite-horizon exponential formulas should accordingly be viewed as analytical benchmarks for finite-horizon implementation.
